messages.subject: stumped by indexing
parts:
Hello everyone,

I have a CMR model where I use individual covariates to estimate 1st year survival (in addition to adult survival but without covariates)

The model runs fine but I would like to derive the mean survival of 1st year birds for each occasion, and the indexing to do so is giving me trouble so I'm writing here to see if anyone has ideas.

Survival for juveniles is indexed as Sj[i,t] in the Nimble model. I had previously run the model using the following to derive average annual 1st year survival (which ran fine):

for(t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
 
    Sj.t[t]<- mean(Sj[1:n.juv,t])
   
  }

However, this returns weird annual survival values for juveniles (while all other parameter estimates are close to the simulated values). I think it may be because Sj exists in all transition matrix slices (i.e., all individuals and all occasions), I think nimble must provide initial values for all these Sj which then get included in my average even if no data informs these nodes and they do not contribute to the likelihood or inform the effect of my covariate (this is my understanding but I realize it may not be exactly that). In any case, I get the wrong annual estimates for Sj. What I want is the average survival for only those individuals that were juveniles in year t. This seemed easy enough but all my attempts at indexing this properly returned errors. Basically, I created a matrix with nrows=number of birds marked per year and ncols=number of marking occasions. This is Sj.pred.index below, and N is the number of birds marked per year. I tried

for(t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
    Sj.t[t]<- mean(Sj[Sj.pred.index[1:N,t],t])
  }

But this returned the error
Error in getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse(x, constNames, indexNames, nimbleFunctionNames, : getSymbolicParentNodesRecurse: only scalar indices are allowed; vector indexing found in Sj[Sj.pred.index[1:4, t], t]

I then tried

for(t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
    Sj.t[t]<- mean(Sj[(min(Sj.pred.index[1:N,t])):(max(Sj.pred.index[1:N,t])),t])
  }

which returned

Dynamic indexing found in a vector of indices, (min(Sj.pred.index[1:4, t])):(max(Sj.pred.index[1:4, t])). Only scalar indices, such as 'idx' in 'x[idx]', can be dynamic. One can instead use dynamic indexing in a vector of indices inside a nimbleFunction.

I have tried a bunch of declinations of this, including esoteric things like the following which computes the correct indices for each time step without referring to matrices or other objects, but to no avail

 for(t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
    Sj.t[t]<- mean(Sj[c((1:N)+N*(t-1)),t])
  }

I realize that using dynamic indexing I may get this done by defining t objects in constants that would hold the proper indices for young marked in each year and refer to each of those objects when computing Sj.t[t] for each t, but this is very clunky and there must be a better way to do this.

I am also joining the model code if anyone wants to give it a go. I realize theres a lot going on, but its just code to simulate data with several pre-determined paramter values modified from the Bayesian Population Ecology book by Kéry & Schaub. The part interesting here is on lines 789-804 in the nimbleCode() call.

Thanks for the help!

Cheers,

Fred

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: stumped by indexing
parts:
Dear Fred,

Thanks for the question.  While not following all the details of your setup, I can make the following suggestion.

You could write a nimbleFunction to do the summation you want.  E.g. you could do something like:

# in the model
for(t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
    Sj.t[t]<- calc_juv_mean(Sj[1:n.juv, t], Sj.pred.index[1:N,t])
  }


# outside the model:
calc_juv_mean <- nimbleFunction(
run = function(Sj_vec = double(1), Sj_pred_index_vec = double(1)) { # all model variables should be doubles, even if they hold integer values
   ans <- 0
   n <- length(Sj_pred_index_vec)
   if(n==0) return(ans)
   for(i in 1:n) {
     ans <- ans + Sj_vec[ Sj_pred_index_vec[i] ]
   }
   ans <- ans/n
   return(ans)
   returnType(double())
}

I haven't tested this code so be sure to check if it's what you need.

Actually I think it should work instead of the for loop to do

ans <- mean( Sj_vec[ Sj_pred_index_vec ] )

but I wrote out the for-loop version  in case it is helpful.  In C++, a compiled for loop should be fast, whereas in R people learn to avoid for loops because they can be slow.  The reason the same code concept in a nimbleFunction should work even when it wouldn't in a model is that nimble must determine a directed acyclic graph from the model declarations, and there are limits to what it will support, as you ran into.  In a nimbleFunction, it just needs to run the imperative (i.e. not declarative) code. So, basically, the suggestion is to use a nimbleFunction to more fully code what you want.

HTH
Perry
